candidate.title: Fake Pet Sale / Puppy Scam
candidate.summary: Scammers post fake online ads for puppies and other pets, take payment for an animal that doesn't exist, then vanish with the money.
safetyTips: Consider adopting from a local rescue or animal shelter instead of buying from an online ad
Research the breeder, rescue, or shelter online before sending any payment, and look for reviews or complaints
Never pay by gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer for a pet purchase since that money is very hard to recover
Insist on picking up the animal yourself or meeting the seller in person rather than relying on shipping
Be skeptical of any request for additional 'permit' or delay fees after you've already paid — legitimate government agencies do not charge fees for pet movement within the U.S.
candidate.howItWorks:
Scammers place attractive ads — especially for purebred puppies — online or on streetcorners, often pricing them far below market value to create urgency to act fast before the animal is "gone." After a buyer agrees to purchase and sends money, the seller may introduce a shipping arrangement with a third-party "transporter" who then contacts the buyer demanding additional upfront fees that keep increasing, sometimes claiming the animal is being held at a stopover and needs a special government permit fee to continue. In reality, no pet exists, no transporter is coming, and every payment sent — whether by gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer — disappears along with the seller.

The FTC notes that after payment, the buyer's supposed pet and the "breeder" simply vanish along with the cash.
redFlags: Prices advertised far below normal cost for the breed to create urgency
Seller pushes you to act fast before the pet is gone
Requests to pay only by gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram
A 'transporter' contacts you after purchase asking for extra, escalating fees for permits, shipping, or a stopover delay
Seller cannot arrange for local pickup or an in-person visit to see the animal
realExamples: FTC's December 2024 consumer alert describing ads for purebred puppies priced at a few hundred dollars when they normally cost thousands, pressuring buyers to act quickly

Indiana State Board of Animal Health warning describing transporters who contact buyers post-sale demanding escalating fees, including a fake claim that the animal is detained during a stopover and needs a government permit fee

New York Department of State's Division of Consumer Protection alert citing reports that a large share of sponsored pet ads may be fake, with buyers losing money or receiving a sick, stolen, or different animal than advertised
candidate.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Getting a pet? Avoid scams" - https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/12/getting-pet-avoid-scams

triage.reasoning: The candidate describes a distinct pet-sale/puppy scam pattern not matching existing shopping scam entries like Fake Online Store or Online Marketplace Buyer Scam. However, the provided source text is a generic FTC consumer alerts page listing unrelated scam topics (car dealership spoofing, tax debt, QR codes, jury duty) and does not actually contain the puppy/pet scam content or the FTC quote claimed in the summary, so the citation cannot be verified against the given source.
